report:
### Conclusion
Scientific research supports the claim: opening a bedroom window or door generally improves sleep quality by increasing ventilation and lowering indoor carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) levels.

### Evidence Summary
In sealed bedrooms, human respiration causes exhaled $\text{CO}_2$ to accumulate throughout the night, often rising above recommended limits ($>1,000\text{ ppm}$). Elevated $\text{CO}_2$ concentrations and stagnant air are linked to reduced deep sleep, increased nighttime awakenings, and lower sleep efficiency.

Field intervention studies and literature reviews show that opening a bedroom door or window improves indoor air exchange, keeping $\text{CO}_2$ levels low. Key findings include:
* **Improved Sleep Efficiency:** Objective tracking (such as actigraphy) indicates reduced sleep latency and fewer disruptions when rooms are well-ventilated.
* **Cognitive Benefits:** Lower overnight $\text{CO}_2$ exposure correlates with reduced morning sleepiness and improved next-day cognitive performance.
* **Perceived Quality:** Participants report cooler, fresher air and higher subjective sleep satisfaction.

### Caveats
Opening external windows can be counterproductive if it exposes the room to high ambient noise, outdoor air pollution, extreme temperatures, or allergens. In those scenarios, opening an interior door or using a air purifier/HVAC fan can provide ventilation without outdoor disturbances.

### Sources

* [Indoor Air Journal Ventilation Study](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/ina.12435)
* [ScienceDirect Bedroom Ventilation Review](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132320306004)
* [Technical University of Denmark (DTU) Research Report](https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day)
